title: Preparing Britain for Disruption: Warnings, Networks and Trust
label: 11 June 2026 · National resilience and communications
summary: The committee questioned Ofcom’s Nihal Newman and disaster-management professor Lee Miles about how prepared UK households and communications services are for emergencies, from power cuts and cyberattacks to war. Miles argued that people tend to focus on immediate household risks and need clear, practical advice delivered through familiar channels. Newman described security rules, backup systems and the need for telecoms, energy providers and government to work together. Both said that preparedness must involve more than government alone; Miles stressed that public trust is essential. They raised concerns about prolonged outages and replacing broadcast television, without reaching a firm verdict on the proposed switch-off.

chapters.title: What risks do people recognise?
chapters.takeaway: People tend to focus on dangers close to home, while national threats can seem distant or hard to act on.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How much do people understand about national and international risks, especially risks to the communications networks we rely on?

evidence.quote: To what extent do you estimate that the public currently have awareness of interconnected national and international risks? Obviously, that includes the ones relating to communications networks, where your special expertise is important for us to hear about. What is the level of awareness of risks in those areas?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Ofcom regulates the companies providing communications services, so we mostly deal with those companies rather than the public. We publish reports about risks and give consumers practical advice, including on replacing older phone networks and avoiding scams.

evidence.quote: Ofcom’s role as a regulator is to enforce the relevant frameworks and legal frameworks that we have, and we monitor industry’s compliance against those frameworks. Therefore, Ofcom’s engagement is predominantly with the industry—with those organisations that we regulate—and there is limited direct engagement with the general public.

That is an annual publication where we set out the risks that the sector faces, plus what we are doing in that space. We also provide guidance and information for consumers. When we think about legacy networks such as the PSTN, we set out in our guidance the sorts of questions that consumers should be asking their operators to help prepare them for that transition, including for scams and fraud—practical tips for people to take; that is information that we make available on our website.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are the companies actually following the security requirements?

evidence.quote: One of your functions, you said, is to monitor industry compliance. How compliant is it?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Operators are taking steps to meet the requirements. We report their progress to the government, but this is ongoing work because the threats keep changing.

evidence.quote: It is a journey, and the threat landscape is evolving. We provide a report to the Secretary of State, and aspects of that have been published by DSIT. We are seeing steps that industry is taking, and they are implementing the measures that we expect them to take in the sector.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: My answer on public awareness is “Not very far at all”. In our 2025 household study, about 52% were aware of all the dangers they faced at home, but about 21% didn’t think they faced, or know of, any risks. That suggests a gap between government priorities and what households recognise.

evidence.quote: “Not very far at all” would be my immediate response to that. I think it is because, when we look at most of the data available in terms of awareness, there is low awareness data among the public, particularly households, about specific types of risks and hazards.

In the 2025 study that we did, something like 52% of households were aware of all the hazards that they faced in their households, but something like 21% did not think they had or were aware of any risks at all. That is an illustration of awareness. The first thing is low awareness, which may be part of the argument. The second is what you might call disconnected priorities—the messaging around resilience coming from the resilience action plan, the national security strategy, the industry strategy and around the ‘whole of society’ approach.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: People mainly worry about dangers that feel personal. In our survey, 35% saw accidents at home as a threat, compared with 4% for terrorism and 5% for war or conflict. About three-quarters reported taking no specific action on climate change. But people increasingly see how international conflicts can raise their energy bills.

evidence.quote: What the data shows is that households, as well as the public in particular, see resilience in a very localised setting, often in their own personal dimension. In the survey study that I was involved in, something like the highest level of perceived threat were accidents at home (35%), and the lowest level, at only 4%, was terrorism, and 5% on conflict and war. You see this disconnection of priorities. That is an important point. In effect, that leads to limited action. Something like 75% of households that we looked at in the study indicated that they took no specific action at all in relation to climate change, for example, and those kinds of elements.

with the Iran war and so forth, there is a rising awareness of what you might call ‘cascading effects’. The public and households have become very much aware that geopolitics leads to higher energy prices, with implications for their standards of living.

turns.speaker: Lord Oates
turns.text: But might the public be judging the risks they actually face quite accurately?

evidence.quote: would you say that those figures were an accurate perception by the public of risks that they face?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: What people notice, what they prepare for and what happens in practice are different things. Risks feel different depending on where someone lives, and the picture varies between urban and rural communities.

evidence.quote: there is often a difference between awareness, if you like, which is perception, action—which can be seen as preparedness—and, if you like, delivery or outcomes.
There is also a very strong regional difference between urban communities and rural communities, about how they would perceive communication around awareness of interconnected hybrid threats.

chapters.title: How to reach people
chapters.takeaway: Warnings need to explain why a risk matters to a household and reach people through the channels they actually use.

turns.speaker: Baroness Northover
turns.text: It makes sense that families worry about accidents at home. How can the government help them prepare for wider risks when different people get information from so many different places?

evidence.quote: accidents in the home, especially with little children, would be high on the agenda and are most likely, so maybe that conclusion that people are coming to appears to be logical.

With a fragmented media landscape, with audiences receiving information from different places, platforms, formats, and that changing as well and being likely to continue to change, how do you get the resilience or preparedness message across in that circumstance?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: People are usually making reasonable judgments about their local risks. Start by explaining why wider threats matter to their own household. Then show the choices they can make, such as protecting a home against flooding or installing fire alarms. Help them act, perhaps through government support schemes or cheaper insurance, and show whether those steps actually make them safer.

evidence.quote: we have to recognise that households and the public are rational actors, for the most part. They are being perfectly rational in deciding what are the threats and hazards for them in their local community—in that dimension.

The first E is what you might call ‘enlightened context’, which is making it clear in government communications why that context is important for the public and the households, to take on the resilience domain.

Resilience is a choice about what they want to do and what they want to invest in. Do they want to invest in flooding measures for their houses, new technology, fire alarms or whatever, in relation to those kinds of elements?

That might mean incentivisation schemes, so that if they undertake resilience actions or buy different types of new technologies, they might see an insurance discount, reduced premium and/or government scheme that might help with that.
The fourth and final element you might call the ‘evaluation of outcomes’ to show that doing this actually leads to an outcome of better resilience.

turns.speaker: Baroness Northover
turns.text: That still leaves the problem of how to get reliable information to people who use social media or private WhatsApp groups instead of government websites or broadcasters.

evidence.quote: 15 to 25 year-olds will be getting their information not from government or broadcasters and so on but from social media platforms. People may be getting their information in WhatsApp groups from their friends and relations and so on. Following up on your four Es, how do you get information over that is reliable, in our view, in those circumstances?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Agree on the essential warning, then adapt it for each audience and platform. A website reaches people already interested, but many others depend on TikTok, Facebook, family or local contacts. Messages must be tailored to those routes, which takes substantial resources.

evidence.quote: I would advocate a hub-and-spoke communications strategy. In effect, the hub is where you are providing a common agreement about what the communication of the threat should be—in other words, what the context should be. The spokes are the delivery across the various platforms according to the different audiences.

We use websites as static places where the interested will go to find out more information. We have large elements of society in households that are not interested or engaged, and the platforms from which they gain information are anything from TikTok all the way through to Facebook and other social media, and anecdotal information, which might be the local community or family. The important thing to realise is that you need bespoke formats and delivery platforms to be able to achieve this. That means that communication on resilience, to put it bluntly, is not a cheap endeavour.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Ofcom also studies how people consume media. I can provide the committee with relevant findings from our Media Nations research.

evidence.quote: Ofcom carries out consumer research, and there is one, specifically Media Nations, which, if the committee is interested, I can follow up and provide the information from, if it will be helpful.

chapters.title: Lessons from other countries
chapters.takeaway: Sweden offers useful ideas, but simpler community warning methods and public trust matter as much as advanced technology.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hunter of Auchenreoch
turns.text: What could Britain learn from Sweden and from your work in Africa and the Caribbean?

evidence.quote: you have had dealings with Sweden. We heard from the Nordic countries on their communications strategies. I know that you have also been in Africa and the Caribbean. I wonder what you could bring to the UK: what experience have you seen out there that might be effective back here?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Sweden gives households printed guidance on preparing for a crisis or war, and it has schemes to help communities prepare. But this works in a country with a long tradition of planning for national emergencies and relatively high trust in government. Britain’s circumstances are different, so we can’t simply copy it.

evidence.quote: there has been a total defence strategy, the legacy of non-alignment and neutrality and a high level of cultural and societal trust in the workings of government. That allows for strategies like hard-copy pamphlet templates, such as the famous In Case of Crisis or War piece from 2018, updated in 2024.
they have also provided standards and incentivisation schemes to allow both households and communities to develop and move forward with various aspects.

If you look there, it is often the case that citizen allegiance and trust in government are much higher than they would be in the UK context. We learn from that perspective, but we also have to recognise that the environmental conditions in the UK are very different.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Japan has a public emergency alert system, and Britain has a similar phone-based warning system. The UK system was tested when Plymouth needed a bomb evacuation, and the Cabinet Office leads it.

evidence.quote: Japan has an emergency alert system, and there is a similar facility in the UK, where we have our cell broadcast, which was launched in early 2003. It was tested and exercised in early 2024 when the Plymouth bomb evacuation needed to happen. I agree that there is a lot more to be done, but we do have some examples over here. The alert system is led by the Cabinet Office.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hunter of Auchenreoch
turns.text: And how do places dealing with floods in Africa or hurricanes in the Caribbean warn people?

evidence.quote: How do they do it in Africa, where there have been all these floods and climate situations? How do they do it in the Caribbean, with their hurricanes?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: In parts of Africa, communities can’t rely on the satellite phones, spare mobile towers and other advanced equipment used in wealthier countries. Local agreements and low-tech tools, such as loudhailers, can be vital. Britain should keep workable fallbacks too, especially in rural areas, as older analogue phone networks may be phased out.

evidence.quote: They have a lot of technological advantages in terms of satellite phones, satellite redundancy situations and mobile networks they can call on, or masts, if they are damaged. You do not have that in the African context.

The African context shows that there is also a very strong reliance on low-tech solutions. As we become more digitalised, the question of single points of failure and redundancy becomes really quite challenging. Where we would have used analogue phones, for example, for a digital breakdown in the UK, we may be moving away from having an analogue telecommunications system as it once was. That in itself creates challenges. Often you find that the strength is in having local communities that might have hailer systems, for example, and communication agreements about how to communicate and do it in the local setting.

As part of building resilience, we should not forget that we do not just need to go high; we need to create redundancy which is lower, particularly in the parts of our communities that are rural and may be outside the communications networks.

chapters.title: If the networks go down
chapters.takeaway: Backup systems exist, but prolonged failures would require power restoration, cooperation with private firms and realistic planning for outages.

turns.speaker: Lord Farmer
turns.text: What happens if a cyberattack cuts off internet communications for days? And if ordinary broadcast television is switched off in 2034, how would emergency warnings reach everyone?

evidence.quote: We have not really looked at the scenario of a total blackout in which it is lost for several days. In 2034, the digital terrestrial television signals will be switched off. What effect might that have on the ability to transmit emergency messaging to the whole population if there was a cyber attack causing a communications blackout?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Ofcom tells phone and internet companies not to let one failed part bring down their whole service. They should have backup power, clear recovery plans and practice using them. The government also has emergency-service communications and access to satellite systems.

evidence.quote: In there, we say to avoid single points of failure: build your infrastructure and architecture in a way that there is an aspect of redundancy; recognise the challenges with that; and, as part of that, have business continuity plans and disaster recovery plans. But within those plans, we say to be very clear what those processes are because often the processes can be there, but they are not understood and they are not tested. We make it clear that we expect the operators to do that. We also expect that there is power resilience. Where are the key sites that the operators should have the power backup?

for government, in the event of a national emergency situation, we have the Emergency Services Network. The Home Office is investing in this across the UK, and it is looking to further harden that network. There are also the satellite communication services available to the UK Government in the event of a national emergency.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: For local outages, operators can bring in temporary mobile equipment and generators. People can use another mobile network to make an emergency call. Some places, including the Shetland Islands, are also investing in satellite equipment for community use.

evidence.quote: they can deploy mobile cell sites. Where there is either a specific incident, an outage or damage to a subsea cable, they can deploy an interim mobile coverage solution for that area. They also have generators on wheels, so they can deploy generators in the areas that need it.
Currently, in the event of an emergency, individuals can roam on to different networks to make an emergency call.
In certain communities, such as the Shetland Islands, we are also seeing investment in satellite terminals that are available to the community.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Restoring electricity quickly is just as important. Ofcom is working with energy companies and telecoms providers so their engineers can coordinate during an outage. We’re drawing lessons from the blackouts in Spain and Portugal.

evidence.quote: to restore the power very swiftly is also very important. Ofcom has been working very closely with the energy sector and industry to establish how communication can improve when there is an incident. How can the telecommunications sector and energy sector engineers communicate and co-ordinate on the ground to ensure the services are restored very swiftly? That work still continues, but we are learning from what happened in Spain and Portugal

turns.speaker: Lord Farmer
turns.text: But what if satellites themselves are destroyed in an attack?

evidence.quote: If we had some satellite disruption—satellite warfare, for example—and all the satellites were destroyed, how does that leave us?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: It depends how widespread the failure is. Fixed lines, mobile networks and satellites provide different options. Once the problem goes beyond one industry, the Cabinet Office has to consider the national response.

evidence.quote:
The point is how wide, because it is a tiered level of resilience.

What is available in the fixed network? What is available in mobile? What is available in satellite? That is where the Government then step in from a national resilience perspective, rather than looking at it from a specific sectoral perspective. That is the role the Cabinet Office plays in this area.

turns.speaker: Baroness Mobarik
turns.text: What share of emergency communications relies on commercial phone and satellite networks? What UK-controlled alternatives would remain if those failed?

evidence.quote: what proportion of the UK’s emergency communications capability is dependent on commercial telecommunications and satellite networks? What sovereign alternatives exist, should those networks fail?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: I’d need to come back with the figures. There’s also an unresolved question about what UK control means: must everything operate inside Britain, or can we rely on trusted international partners? We’re building extra safeguards and partnerships.

evidence.quote: On the facts about proportions, I am happy to come back on that point. Sovereignty is a very interesting point and a discussion that is pretty alive at the moment. It comes down to what we mean by sovereignty. Are we talking about trusted partners and nations, or are we looking at just working within the jurisdiction of the nation? That dialogue is continuing at this moment, but we are seeing that in the UK we are building those layers of resilience for ourselves. We are building those necessary partnerships that the UK requires, which is the key thing for us.

turns.speaker: Baroness Curran
turns.text: Have you actually planned for a wartime attack that badly damages our communications?

evidence.quote: Has Ofcom game-planned the possibility of a war situation, if we were attacked and it was a very serious attack on our communications? Do you have emergencies for that kind of extreme situation?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: The government department responsible for telecoms, DSIT, leads that kind of planning. Ofcom joins its discussions.

evidence.quote: DSIT is the policy owner for telecommunications and carries out the cross-sectoral risk scenario that you are describing. We join those conversations with DSIT and participate.

turns.speaker: Baroness Curran
turns.text: So has that work actually been done?

evidence.quote: Have you done that? Has that been done?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: We work with DSIT, the Cabinet Office and industry on those scenarios.

evidence.quote: We work with them in that space, including with the Cabinet Office and industry. We also work with the industry bodies that play a part in that. So, yes, we do engage in those conversations.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: We also need to think about how long failures last. Caribbean hurricanes have taken communications networks out for two weeks, and I cited a power outage that affected 80% of Cuba for eight months after hurricanes Irma and Maria. For households and small businesses, internet access is an essential service, so the public needs realistic expectations of recovery times.

evidence.quote: There are very good examples in the Caribbean of hurricanes that have knocked out entire communications networks for two weeks at a time. In the case of Cuba after Irma and Maria, there was a power outage for 80% of the island for eight months.

For many people—SMEs, the business community, local communities and households—the internet is not optional; it is a way of life and an essential service. We need to be very clear about treating the length of disruption to an essential service as something that requires management of expectations, both nationally and for our service providers.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Private companies carry out most emergency recovery work. Agreements with them must cover how their costs will be paid when recovery lasts longer than the immediate response.

evidence.quote: the vast majority of our recovery and response is delivered by private sector providers. It is often the case that 80% of recovery is provided by the private sector. The arrangements between those providers is important, not just over the short-term response phase but the longer-term recovery phase, because there are costs that have to be met commercially if those services are to continue to be provided beyond MoUs.

chapters.title: Education and cybersecurity rules
chapters.takeaway: Education and training can improve preparedness, while security rules must cover major operators and connected services without falling behind new threats.

turns.speaker: Lord Oates
turns.text: What should schools, colleges and universities do to help people prepare for emergencies?

evidence.quote: Could you share your views about the role that the education sector, at all levels, should play in promoting preparedness and resilience to a wide audience?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Schools can teach children how to respond to emergencies, as happens in places regularly hit by disasters. Young people also influence how families prepare and may become future volunteers.

evidence.quote: if we look at the school level, there are lots of initiatives and work on smart schools, in which the idea is to build resilience—understanding resilience, basic resilience, response ideas and how to do things—into the curriculum. That is very common in places such as the Caribbean where there is a continual threat.

it often has an important impact at home, in the household, where resilience influencers are in the teenage group. From a school perspective, we need to understand that 14 to 25 year-olds—if I may use that age bracket, which is beyond full school age—since these are the future volunteers on whom resilience will be based.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Further education colleges could offer practical training such as first aid, including to older adults. Universities can research which preparations work, train professional emergency planners and work with businesses on practical solutions.

evidence.quote: The FE level has a substantial role in widening access. What I mean by that is that FE colleges and provision do not just teach key subjects such as geography, where things such as hurricanes and earthquakes are part of the normal curriculum. Think about the access and competence courses that are provided, from boot camps to widening-access courses. There is a very strong market, particularly among the, say, 55 to 70 generation, who are interested in those resilience courses. It might also be the place where you find first-aid courses and basic issues to do with training, competencies and skills.

At university level, it is absolutely essential, because our role is providing research about resilience and how it is evaluated in that piece. It is about building the knowledge and thinking. I am also a professor at a disaster management centre who trains emergency planners across the world. Universities have a fundamental role in training emergency planners

working, as I do, with companies including SMEs through to large multinationals, on resilience projects where the public-private partnerships are critical in providing the knowledge with commercial opportunities to deliver the competencies, skills, toolkits and markets of the future.

turns.speaker: Lord Peach
turns.text: Are Britain’s cyber defences as strong as the government suggests? And are national emergency exercises frequent and demanding enough?

evidence.quote: If we turn to cybersecurity, on which the Government are proud of their efforts, do you agree that they should be? How does the telecommunications industry look? You have raised a couple of times what I might call exercising at the national level. Is that frequent enough and are the scenarios tough enough?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: The Telecommunications (Security) Act was introduced in 2021 after specialists assessed risks to the sector. All operators have legal duties, but the detailed security code focuses on medium and large companies because their risks are greater. Ofcom checks progress and reports to the government.

evidence.quote: Telecommunications (Security) Act because it is a key, comprehensive framework that we have in place. It was introduced in 2021 and came about off the back of a risk assessment and a threat assessment carried out by the National Cyber Security Centre.

Ofcom has a key role in that space. We monitor industry compliance and report to the Secretary of State in DSIT on how the sector is performing. One thing that is important with that framework is that it is proportionate. The code of practice is not applicable to everybody, because there are large communication providers with turnovers greater than £1 billion, and much smaller operators as well. The UK Government segmented the market and said that the code of practice would be applicable to the large and medium-sized operators, because the risks they face are much larger and therefore there are different measures that they need to take and timetables that they need to follow.
The Telecommunications (Security) Act is applicable to all telecoms operators.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Companies are investing to meet those requirements, but threats keep changing and the rules need updating. Wider internet infrastructure, including data centres, also needs protection. We coordinate with regulators in other industries and with international partners because failures can spread between sectors.

evidence.quote: What we are observing with those operators is a level of commitment to investing in the requirements that they have to follow. It is a journey—the risk landscape evolves and changes—and we have to ensure that any framework we put in place moves with the threat landscape.

We are expecting data centres to come in, and they will be a key part of that value chain. When we think about communications, we think about subsea cables, satellite communications, terrestrial networks and, now, data centres, as they come in.

We work very closely with other regulators. In the energy sector, with Ofgem, we work with the Information Commissioner’s Office. We work with the CAA in the aviation sector. Nationally, we are working across the board, and we also work with international partners.

turns.speaker: Baroness Winterton of Doncaster
turns.text: Why would data centres need to be covered by the proposed Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill? What would this law add to the rules we already have?

evidence.quote: You talked about data centres. It is not quite clear to me why a data centre needs to be in legislation, but you might expand on that a little. Do either of you have reflections on that Bill? Crucially, what extras will it bring?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Data centres are important to the UK’s plans for artificial intelligence, so the Bill proposes giving Ofcom responsibility for overseeing their security. It would also look at suppliers that different essential services depend on, not just the suppliers within one industry.

evidence.quote: The data infrastructure sector was designated as critical national infrastructure. It is pivotal for us in the UK when we think about AI and our AI growth and ambitions in that space. So, having an aspect of security and resilience oversight is important for us.
It is the oversight that has been proposed in the legislation. Ofcom is named as the regulator in the legislation.

The first is supply chain risks. We are seeing supply chains and the compromise of our supply chains filtering through all different industries. That is one aspect coming through in the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill. We are not just thinking about critical suppliers within our sectors but also across the sectors. At the moment, we look at our suppliers within our sectors. The Bill looks at not only the risks within your sector and your critical suppliers, but also across the sectors.

turns.speaker: Baroness Winterton of Doncaster
turns.text: Would the Bill make companies follow new rules, or simply let someone monitor them?

evidence.quote: Is it regulation or monitoring that is in the Bill?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Much of the detail will come later in further regulations. The proposals draw on the existing Cyber Assessment Framework, a method for checking organisations’ security, and include faster reporting of incidents so regulators can see where problems are emerging.

evidence.quote: The detail will come in secondary legislation. The proposals at this moment involve looking at the risks around supply chains. The Government’s ambition is dealing with those risks. They are also looking at the specific requirements. Where the Bill reflects on existing frameworks, the National Cyber Security Centre has the Cyber Assessment Framework, which is peppered throughout the cyber Bill.

Finally, learning from other countries, incident reporting is important. If we do not have the data in a timely fashion, we do not have that evidence and we do not know where our risks are. That is another proposal that the Government have put in the Bill.

turns.speaker: Baroness Mobarik
turns.text: What about smaller operators? Small businesses are also facing more cyber threats.

evidence.quote: your focus is on the security of the larger telecoms providers, but we have heard that there is an increasing level of threat to SMEs. Are you looking at that? How are you proposing to strengthen that?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: The law covers all telecoms operators. Our main checks focus on providers with annual turnover above £50 million, for whom the detailed code was designed. But we also speak to smaller operators, including through industry groups, and point them to security guidance.

evidence.quote: The Telecommunications (Security) Act is applicable to all telecoms operators. Our focus is on those operators that have a turnover greater than £50 million, because the code of practice is designed for that size of operations. But at the same time, where there are opportunities, we engage with the smaller operators, even through industry bodies, and encourage them to look at the code of practice.

There is also quite a bit of information and guidance for smaller operators, which the NCSC publishes on its website. When there is an issue, concern or incident, we engage with the smaller operators as well.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Common minimum standards are helpful, but guidance must adapt quickly to changing attacks, including those using AI. I cited figures suggesting 60% to 70% of UK small and medium-sized businesses have experienced a cyberattack. Leaders also need to understand why investing in protection matters, not just leave it to technical staff.

evidence.quote: The Bill is encouraging in having baseline expectations and creating sector standards, which are very important—and inter-sector standards, which is the implication of what is being talked about. The important thing to also recognise is that the codes of practice that follow need to be agile enough to take into account that the sector itself is moving at great pace, particularly around AI and other domains. For example, I was struck that most recent data shows that 60% to 70% of SMEs in the UK have experienced a cyberattack

there is a big piece of work not just about how we train or exercise the Bill and its implications but about educating our senior management teams in the strategic value of investment beyond the regulation. That is very important.

turns.speaker: Baroness Winterton of Doncaster
turns.text: If we have to wait for the detailed regulations before people can be trained, won’t that slow everything down?

evidence.quote: if we are waiting for all this secondary legislation, and if training will not start until the secondary legislation is there, I am a bit anxious as to whether that becomes a delay. Is there any danger in that?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: We aren’t starting from zero. Ofcom already uses the Cyber Assessment Framework, even though the Bill would put parts of the approach into law. We’re also reviewing whether existing rules accidentally hinder companies from using AI to defend against attacks.

evidence.quote: We already apply that framework, so we are already setting those expectations in the way we are engaging with our sector, and other sectors are adopting the framework, because NCSC developed it a couple of years ago. We want to make sure that these frameworks are put on a legal footing, but that does not mean we have not been using them. That is the key difference. It has already started to be applied.

We recently published our approach to AI, and in there is a piece of work that we are doing around looking at our existing regimes to ensure that we are not creating inadvertent barriers around the adoption of AI as defensive tools. We are doing that piece of work this year.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Training is already happening too. It needs to cover both the practical response to attacks and senior managers’ decisions about investing in protection.

evidence.quote: It is not a case of it having not started; it is already going all the time, because cybersecurity threats are a constant aspect in relation to that. Of course, as the legislation moves forward, this creates new environments and new expectations, so it is about raising that game. But I also think that, from this perspective, it is about the linkage between what you might call resilience management—training managers in the industry of the value of cybersecurity and the investment—alongside the operational aspects of defending and operationalising it.

turns.speaker: Baroness Winterton of Doncaster
turns.text: Can you train senior managers and technical teams together?

evidence.quote: Do you think you can get the two tracks running together?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: We have to. At Bournemouth University, we run exercises that make people at different management levels work through simulated emergencies together.

evidence.quote: They have to run together. At Bournemouth University, if I may use my own example, we have the Disaster Management Centre and the Cyber Competence Centre, and we plan and run operational and strategic courses where we build scenarios that go up and down the management chain to understand that investment and value opportunity.

chapters.title: Keeping everyone informed
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses urged caution about losing broadcast television and ended by calling for cooperation and public trust.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would ending digital terrestrial television make it harder to reach older people, rural communities or anyone with poor internet access? Should the plan be reconsidered?

evidence.quote: this plan to switch off digital terrestrial television in a few years’ time is sensible or completely undesirable, given the concern expressed that it would reduce universal access to information and have a particularly disproportionate adverse impact on certain vulnerable communities or groups of people, such as older people who do not necessarily know what to do with broadband and or do not have very good internet connections? Is this a sensible thing? Are we past the point of no return on the proposal? Is it reversible, and should it be?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Removing a widely used television signal would create a real problem unless its replacement could reliably reach those audiences. We already have rural areas with poor digital coverage. Any replacement needs to work around the clock and have a backup if it fails.

evidence.quote: There is, no doubt, a challenge if you remove that terrestrial facility, which is used by a large demographic of society; we would need to have very clear assurances as to what it would be replaced with as an effective strategy for resilience.

There are many communication channels, which affect rural communities and local communities, where you have dead spots and issues to do with digital delivery. We would have to considerably raise our expectations around a 24/7 delivery or a delivery of core services that is robust enough to provide redundancy if that system is taken out.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Technology is changing, so we should look at the options. But whatever replaces existing systems must be dependable, with extra safeguards where particular communities need them.

evidence.quote: Technology is evolving, and that is the key thing: we need to look at how it is, what the opportunities are and how we can harness those. The second, I agree, is around ensuring the resilience of whatever we roll out, looking at what the different areas and communities require and targeting any additional enhanced resilience requirements for those as well.

turns.speaker: Baroness Helic
turns.text: What single recommendation would each of you make to the government?

evidence.quote: if there were one recommendation that you could make to the Government on resilience and preparedness, what would that be?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Make it clear what preparing the whole country really involves, and bring government, businesses, researchers and communities together to work on it. No one sector can solve these problems alone.

evidence.quote: We cannot work within our silos. We need to continue to work across the sector, and with communities, industry and academia. My recommendation would be that we need to be clear what we mean by the whole-society approach and we need to bring everybody around the table to work together.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: The central issue is trust. People need advice they believe and steps that make sense in everyday household life. We can learn from Sweden, but those lessons won’t work here unless we address the public’s confidence in institutions.

evidence.quote: we have to deal with the question of building trust, which is central to this.

we have a society that has issues of trust in messaging and communication from our institutions. We need to invest and understand what we mean by everyday resilience that makes sense to the households and the publics of our country and, on the basis of that, most importantly, can build trust. Without trust, there is no point in looking at states such as Sweden or others.
